title: Every Tate ideal admits best approximation for the Gauss norm
statement:
Let $K$ be a field [def-weil-field], complete for a nontrivial real-valued nonarchimedean absolute value, and let $s\ge0$. Let $T_s=K\langle X_1,\ldots,X_sangle$ be the restricted-series ring [def-trf-restricted-series-presentation], consisting of coefficient families $\sum_
u a_
u X^
u$ for which only finitely many $|a_
u|\ge\epsilon$ for each $\epsilon>0$, with Gauss norm $\|f\|_G=\sup_
u|a_
u|$. For every ideal $I\subseteq T_s$ and every $f\in T_s$ there is $g\in I$ such that $\|f-g\|_G\le\|f-h\|_G$ for every $h\in I$. Equivalently, the infimum defining the Gauss quotient norm on each coset of $T_s/I$ is attained by a representative of that coset. The ideals $I=(0)$ and $I=T_s$ and the case $s=0$ are included; neither reducedness of $T_s/I$ nor algebraic closedness of $K$ is assumed.

source.place: Corollary 5.2.7/8, strict closedness of Tate ideals (best approximation formulation). BGR is absent locally, so its proof and full printed wording remain WANTED. Corroboration read online in Jakob Werner, Coherent Sheaves on Non-Archimedean Analytic Spaces, Corollary 3.4.8 proof, printed p.57: strict closedness yields surjectivity onto the quotient-norm unit ball. This is a statement-only analytic input, not a claim to have read the BGR proof.

proof.text: Use the graded lexicographic order and $L(u)$ of [lem-trf-tate-convergent-division]. A nonzero restricted series has positive Gauss norm attained at finitely many coefficients: choose one nonzero coefficient of modulus $a>0$; the set of coefficients of modulus at least $a$ is finite and contains the maximum of all coefficients. Put $D=\{L(u):0\ne u\in I\}$. By [lem-trf-dickson-exponent-sequences], $D$ has a finite subset $B$ such that every $\nu\in D$ dominates some $\beta\in B$ componentwise. Indeed, if no finite subset works, recursively choose $\beta_n\in D$ which dominates none of $\beta_0,\ldots,\beta_{n-1}$. The cited sequence-pair property supplies $m<n$ with $\beta_m\le\beta_n$, a contradiction. This also gives $B=\varnothing$ when $I=(0)$.

source.place: Agent proof of BGR Corollary 5.2.7/8 by finite leading exponents and bounded convergent division. BGR absent locally; Bosch Lectures on Formal and Rigid Geometry §1.3 Corollary 9 (printed p.21) checked online for the exact conclusion, not used as an unproved invocation.

proof.text: For each $\beta\in B$, choose $0\ne u_\beta\in I$ with $L(u_\beta)=\beta$. Divide $u_\beta$ by its coefficient at $\beta$ to get $b_\beta\in I$ with norm one and the same leading exponent. Apply [lem-trf-tate-convergent-division] to this finite list and $f$. Write $f=\sum_{\beta\in B}q_\beta b_\beta+r$, and put $g=\sum_{\beta\in B}q_\beta b_\beta\in I$. Every exponent occurring in $r$ fails to dominate every $\beta\in B$.

source.place: Agent proof of BGR Corollary 5.2.7/8 by finite leading exponents and bounded convergent division. BGR absent locally; Bosch Lectures on Formal and Rigid Geometry §1.3 Corollary 9 (printed p.21) checked online for the exact conclusion, not used as an unproved invocation.

proof.text: If $r=0$, the chosen $g=f$ has distance zero and is optimal. Otherwise put $R=\|r\|_G>0$. For $h\in I$ put $k=h-g\in I$. Suppose $\|f-h\|_G=\|r-k\|_G<R$. At every exponent where the coefficient of $r$ has modulus $R$, the coefficient of $k$ has modulus $R$ by the ultrametric inequality; at every other exponent the coefficient of $k$ has modulus less than $R$. Thus $k\ne0$, $\|k\|_G=R$, and its maximal-norm exponents are exactly those of $r$, so $L(k)=L(r)$. Since $L(k)\in D$, some $\beta\in B$ satisfies $\beta\le L(r)$, contradicting the support condition from step 2. Therefore $\|f-g\|_G=R\le\|f-h\|_G$ for every $h\in I$. The coset representatives are exactly the $f-h$, so this is also attainment of their infimum. The same argument includes $s=0$; for $I=T_s$ one can alternatively take $g=f$.
